This vignette works through the Lab 4 group tasks. Part 1 estimates the
proportion of people who think the work scientists do benefits them
(`global_monitor`, where the true proportion is 0.80). Part 2 builds a
confidence interval for the proportion of US adults who think climate
change is affecting their local community (`us_adults`, true proportion
0.62). Every random draw uses a fixed seed (`sample_props()` applies it
via `withr::with_seed()`), so all numbers here are reproducible.

```{r populations}
table(global_monitor$scientist_work)
table(us_adults$climate_change_affects)
```

# Part 1: Sampling distributions

Task 1 takes a single sample of size 20. Task 2 and Task 3 repeat that
sampling 2000 times to build sampling distributions for n = 20 and
n = 200 and compare their shape and spread.

## Task 1: one sample of size 20

```{r task-1}
p_hat1 <- sample_props(global_monitor, "scientist_work", "Benefits",
  size = 20, reps = 1, seed = 42
)
p_hat1
```

In this sample, `r round(p_hat1 * 20)` of the 20 people think the work
scientists do enhances their lives, so the sample proportion is
p-hat = `r p_hat1`.

**Point estimate:** the point estimate of the population proportion of
people who think the work scientists do enhances their lives is
p-hat = `r p_hat1` (90%). A different student's sample would generally
give a different point estimate -- with only 20 people, sample
proportions are quite variable.

## Task 2: 2000 samples of size 20

```{r task-2}
sample_props20 <- sample_props(global_monitor, "scientist_work", "Benefits",
  size = 20, reps = 2000, seed = 42
)
hist(sample_props20,
  breaks = seq(0.35, 1.05, by = 0.05),
  col = "grey85",
  main = "Sampling distribution of p-hat, n = 20",
  xlab = "Sample proportion (p-hat)"
)
summary(sample_props20)
```

The distribution is centred near the true proportion (mean =
`r round(mean(sample_props20), 4)`), but it is not symmetric: the
smallest p-hat is `r min(sample_props20)` while the largest is
`r max(sample_props20)`, and `r round(100 * mean(sample_props20 == 1), 1)`%
of samples hit the ceiling of exactly 1. The left tail stretches far
below the centre (first quartile = `r quantile(sample_props20, 0.25)`)
while only a thin sliver sits above 0.9. Because the true proportion is
high (0.80) and the samples are small, the right side is truncated at 1
and a long left tail develops.

**Answer: Yes, the data are left skewed.**

## Task 3: 2000 samples of size 200

```{r task-3}
sample_props200 <- sample_props(global_monitor, "scientist_work", "Benefits",
  size = 200, reps = 2000, seed = 42
)
hist(sample_props200,
  breaks = seq(0.65, 0.95, by = 0.01),
  col = "grey85",
  main = "Sampling distribution of p-hat, n = 200",
  xlab = "Sample proportion (p-hat)"
)
c(mean = mean(sample_props200), sd = sd(sample_props200))
```

With n = 200 the distribution is centred on the true proportion again
(mean = `r round(mean(sample_props200), 4)`) but this time it is roughly
symmetric with no visible ceiling effect, since typical samples sit far
from 1.

**What value would you use to estimate the true population proportion?**

**Answer: The mean of the sample proportions.** The mean of the 2000
proportions is `r round(mean(sample_props200), 4)`, essentially the
known truth of 0.80: the mean of a sampling distribution of p-hat equals
the population proportion it estimates.

**Which sampling distribution has a smaller spread?**

**Answer: The sampling distribution from Q3** (n = 200). Its standard
deviation is `r round(sd(sample_props200), 4)` versus
`r round(sd(sample_props20), 4)` for n = 20 -- larger samples produce
sample proportions that cluster more tightly around the truth, in line
with sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n).

# Confidence intervals

The Wald interval for a proportion is p-hat +/- z* x
sqrt(p-hat * (1 - p-hat) / n), where z* is the critical value carrying
the confidence level in the middle of the standard normal curve.

**For a confidence level of 90%, what is the appropriate critical value?**

```{r critical-value}
z_star <- stats::qnorm(0.95)
z_star
```

**Answer: z* = 1.64** (to 2 decimal places; `r round(z_star, 4)`
unrounded). The remaining 10% error probability splits evenly across
the two tails, so the critical value is the normal distribution's
0.95 quantile.

## Task 4: a 90% confidence interval from a sample of size 60

```{r task-4}
p_hat4 <- sample_props(us_adults, "climate_change_affects", "Yes",
  size = 60, reps = 1, seed = 312
)
p_hat4

ci90 <- prop_ci(p_hat4, size = 60, conf_level = 0.90)
ci90
```

The sample proportion is p-hat = `r round(p_hat4, 4)` (of the 60 adults
sampled, `r round(p_hat4 * 60)` think climate change is affecting their
local community), and the 90% confidence interval runs from
`r round(ci90$lower, 4)` to `r round(ci90$upper, 4)`.

**Interpretation:** we are 90% confident that the true proportion of US
adults who think climate change is affecting their local community is
between `r round(ci90$lower, 4)` and `r round(ci90$upper, 4)`. This
particular interval does capture the known population truth of 0.62 --
each new sample gives its own interval, and about 90% of those
intervals will contain the true proportion.

**Is this interval narrower or wider than the earlier 95% confidence
interval?**

```{r compare-cis}
ci95 <- prop_ci(p_hat4, size = 60, conf_level = 0.95)
ci95
rbind(
  width_90 = c(
    lower = ci90$lower, upper = ci90$upper,
    width = ci90$upper - ci90$lower
  ),
  width_95 = c(
    lower = ci95$lower, upper = ci95$upper,
    width = ci95$upper - ci95$lower
  )
)
```

**Answer: narrower.** The same sample gives a 95% interval of width
`r round(ci95$upper - ci95$lower, 4)` but a 90% interval of width only
`r round(ci90$upper - ci90$lower, 4)`: lowering the confidence level
shrinks the critical value from `r round(ci95$critical_value, 2)` to
`r round(ci90$critical_value, 2)`, so the interval tightens. That is
the confidence-precision trade-off -- to be more confident, the
interval must be wider.
